clue.text: Greek's equine haunch photo

blocks.note: the haunch is the hip and buttock area
pic is short for picture

explanation.surface: A snapshot of a Greek horse's hindquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is built from the Greek hippos, horse, which is why the definition credits the Greeks.
explanation.definitionFit: The rare adjective means relating to horses or horse racing, formed from the Greek noun for horse.

clue.text: Revolutionary addressing African dictator of little brain

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase for a noun: read it as 'one of little brain'

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a letter addressed to someone is written 'to' them
Idi Amin, the Ugandan dictator

explanation.surface: A rebel writing to a tyrant who is not very bright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a noun for a rebel, but it only tells you to turn the letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with little brain is stupid, and a fool or dimwit is exactly what the noun names.

clue.text: Fish like cod don't have tails cut up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom, so the order flips

blocks.note: to lop is to cut off, as when tails are docked
to lack something is not to have it

explanation.surface: Some fish resembling cod have had their tails chopped off.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is read backwards from the end of the clue: the cut comes first once turned, then what the fish don't have.
explanation.definitionFit: This North Atlantic food fish belongs to the cod family and looks much like its cousin.

clue.text: Worker putting nail through tongue, perhaps nurse keeps confined

definitions.text: Worker putting nail through tongue, perhaps

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it within, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a carer looks after the sick, as a nurse does
pent, as in pent up, means shut in

explanation.surface: A gruesome image of someone nailing through a tongue while a nurse is kept shut away.
explanation.walkthrough: The tongue is not in a mouth: tongue and groove is a woodworking joint, which makes the long definition fair and witty.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodworker joining boards may drive a nail through the tongue of a tongue-and-groove joint.

clue.text: Injure heel on driver's side

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another follows it, so the first-named part goes second

blocks.note: in Britain the off side of a car is the right, the driver's side
the heel is the end of a loaf or of the foot

explanation.surface: Hurting your heel on the driver's side of a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the heel after the side in an across clue. The off side is the side away from the kerb, the driver's side in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: To injure someone's feelings or pride is to wound them emotionally, the usual sense of the verb.

clue.text: Sweet Glaswegian's bottom ogled regularly

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is taken

blocks.note: fud is Scottish slang for the backside
second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A sweet-natured Scot whose backside is being eyed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' here is the noun, the confectionery, not a compliment to the Glaswegian.
explanation.definitionFit: This soft confection of sugar, butter and milk is a classic British sweet or candy.

clue.text: European back from China, say

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
astern means at or towards the back of a ship

explanation.surface: A European returning home from a trip to China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back from China' reads as a return trip, but 'back' belongs with the wordplay and 'from China, say' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: China is an example of a country of the Orient, so something originating there is oriental.

clue.text: Find nothing really under layer of cartilage

indicators.note: in a down clue, what lies under comes lower, so the first-named part is written second

blocks.note: a spinal disc is a pad of cartilage between vertebrae
zero, nothing
very and really are both intensifiers

explanation.surface: Locating nothing at all beneath a layer of cartilage, as in a disappointing scan.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'under' places the second part below the first. 'Find' is a noun here, as in a great find.
explanation.definitionFit: A find is something unearthed or come upon, and the noun for that event or object is a synonym.

clue.text: E.g. ass working Bude seafront, carrying British

indicators.note: letters that are working are in motion and get rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written; Bude is a Cornish seaside town
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A donkey giving rides on the Cornish seafront at Bude, laden with a Briton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carrying' means the British letter goes in with the rest before the whole lot is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A donkey is a classic example of an animal used for carrying loads, so the definition is by example.

clue.text: Steady hands split bananas in fridge

indicators.note: going bananas is going crazy, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: split into left and right hands, L and R
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone holding sliced bananas steady in the fridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steady' looks like an adjective or an order, but it is the noun for a regular partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Going steady means dating one person regularly, so one's steady is a regular romantic partner.

clue.text: A couple of stitches in your ear, tolerable

indicators.note: what reaches the ear is the sound, not the spelling

blocks.note: two stitches are two sews

explanation.surface: Getting a couple of stitches in your ear was bearable.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a medical wound; the stitches are sewing, said twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Something merely passable or neither good nor bad is described with this informal reduplicated word.

clue.text: A kid with feet up, perhaps

blocks.note: taken as written
to kid someone is to tease them

explanation.surface: A child lounging with its feet up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a child, but it is the verb meaning to joke with someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting your feet up is an example of relaxing, being comfortable and untroubled.

clue.text: Half of drawing revealed secret bones

indicators.note: taking only half means the rest of the word is dropped

blocks.note: a sketch is a drawing; its first half is kept
to let on is to reveal a secret

explanation.surface: A half-finished drawing that gave away hidden bones, like an X-ray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revealed secret' is a single phrasal verb, let on, not an adjective and noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole framework of bones in a body is the meaning of this anatomical noun.

clue.text: Member on visit to zoo saving unknown parrot

indicators.note: saving means except, so something is left out

blocks.note: member is a euphemism for the penis, of which this is slang
visiting a place, you are at it
zoo without Z, the unknown
x, y and z are the algebraic unknowns; this one is removed

explanation.surface: A club member on a zoo trip rescuing a mystery parrot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saving' looks like rescuing but means except. An unknown in algebra is x, y or z.
explanation.definitionFit: This crested Australasian bird is a member of the parrot order.

clue.text: 13 expert thought a poet's oesophagus somewhat twisted

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the text is used
twisted round, the run of letters faces the other way

blocks.note: the letters run across the word breaks

explanation.surface: Someone reckoned a poet's gullet was a bit contorted.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 refers to the answer to 13 across, SKELETON, so the definition is a bone specialist.
explanation.definitionFit: This practitioner treats the body by manipulating the bones and joints, so is a specialist in the skeleton.

clue.text: London suburb close to Ruislip, nearer the heart

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so the final letter is taken

blocks.note: the final letter
inner means closer to the centre

explanation.surface: A London suburb beside Ruislip, closer to the city centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to Ruislip' reads as geography, and is true: both are in north-west London. In the wordplay 'close' is the end of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: This district in the borough of Harrow is a residential suburb in north-west London.

clue.text: Wearing PE kit, lower leg's very cold

indicators.note: something worn goes round the wearer, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: taken as written
a rig is an outfit or set of equipment
the shin is the front of the lower leg

explanation.surface: A schoolchild in PE kit complaining that their legs are freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'lower leg's' is 'is': the shin is wearing the kit.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal usage calls bitterly chilly weather this, as if one might die of it.

clue.text: Pothead skinned knee in brief rage

indicators.note: skinning removes the outer layer, so the outside letters go
brief means cut short, so the last letter goes
one piece placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: a storm is a rage, here cut short
the word with its outer letters peeled off

explanation.surface: A cannabis user who grazed a knee in a short-lived tantrum.
explanation.walkthrough: Two clipped words: the inner part of one sits inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang for someone who habitually smokes cannabis.

clue.text: Unable to feel American casualty's digits?

blocks.note: numb means without sensation
ER, the emergency room, is the US name for a casualty department; plus the 's

explanation.surface: A US casualty whose fingers have lost all feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain casualty is the hospital's emergency department, which Americans call the ER. The question mark admits that digits here are figures, not fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: Digits are the figures nought to nine, which are the symbols used to write values.

clue.text: Costa recalled seedy nuts, as seen below

indicators.note: to be called back is to come back the way it went
nuts means crazy, so the letters go haywire

blocks.note: costa is the anatomical Latin for a rib
taken as written

explanation.surface: Costa coffee shops have recalled some dodgy nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Costa' looks like the coffee chain, but it is the anatomist's word for a rib, fitting the bones theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird's-eye view looks down from above, so it is how things below appear from high up.

clue.text: Parasite in nose GP treated right

indicators.note: treated means processed or worked on, so the letters are changed

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A family doctor rightly treating a parasite found in a nose.
explanation.walkthrough: A GP is a general practitioner, a family doctor. 'Parasite' is the person who lives off others, not the bug.
explanation.definitionFit: A freeloader who lives off other people's money or generosity is figuratively a parasite.

clue.text: Traveller's stomach flipped during arrival

indicators.note: flipped over, the letters run the other way
something happening during something else falls within it

blocks.note: a comer is one who arrives
tum is a childish word for the stomach

explanation.surface: A traveller's stomach turning over when they arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', linking definition and wordplay, not a possessive. Arrival stands for a person who arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who journeys regularly between home and work is a particular kind of traveller.

clue.text: Growth on lip hurt after time

indicators.note: what comes after is written later, so the first-named part goes second

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to ache is to hurt

explanation.surface: A cold sore on the lip that started hurting after a while.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'after' puts the hurt below the time. Tache is British slang for a moustache.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair grown on the upper lip is a moustache, shortened in informal British speech.

clue.text: Cosmo doctored front of Heidi's neck

indicators.note: doctored means tampered with, so the letters are altered
the front of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: taken as written; Cosmo is Cosmopolitan magazine
the opening letter

explanation.surface: A magazine retouched a photo of Heidi's neck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neck' looks like a body part, in keeping with the theme, but it is the verb meaning to kiss and cuddle.
explanation.definitionFit: To neck is informal for kissing amorously, and the answer is a synonymous verb for that.

clue.text: Vulgar Conservative showing too much cheek?

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
rude means impudent, cheeky; and showing your cheeks is indecent

explanation.surface: A coarse Tory politician being far too cheeky.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the double sense of cheek: impudence, and the buttock, in keeping with the body theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse, offensive or lacking taste: both adjectives describe bad-mannered, indecent behaviour.

clue.text: Every so often my ankles turn

indicators.note: every so often means at intervals, so alternate letters are taken

blocks.note: first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Someone complaining that their ankles keep turning over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' suggests a twisted ankle, but it is the verb meaning become, as in 'she'll make a fine doctor'.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn into something is to become it, and one sense of the answer is to become or develop into.

clue.text: Red footballer repelled attack, getting the bit between his teeth?

indicators.note: to be repelled is to be driven back, so the letters go backwards

blocks.note: Che Guevara, the Marxist revolutionary
a wing is a player on the flank
to mug someone is to assault and rob them

explanation.surface: A Manchester United or Liverpool player driving back an attack with real determination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting the bit between his teeth' is an idiom for determination; read literally, it is something chewed. Red is a left-wing revolutionary.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of this sweet is literally a small bit held and worked between the teeth.

clue.text: Hare isn't missing any toes, perhaps

blocks.note: if none are missing, you have them
a full set of toes numbers ten

explanation.surface: A hare with all its toes intact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hare' is not the animal but the verb meaning to run fast. Someone missing no toes has the full count of them.
explanation.definitionFit: To hare off is British informal for running at great speed, so to hurry or go quickly.

clue.text: Strap around thigh compressing artery walls

indicators.note: walls enclose, so the text is wrapped round the letters wanted

blocks.note: the run of letters spans the two words

explanation.surface: A tight band round the leg squeezing the blood vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artery walls' looks like anatomy, but 'walls' is a verb: the phrase before it walls in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: This elastic band worn round the leg holds up a stocking or sock.
